public_rationale: The tested point is his rebuttal: not every AI data center has locked-in customer demand. CBRE's H1 2026 report says just over 80% of capacity under construction in the main North American markets was preleased. That leaves up to about 1,500 MW with no tenant. A June 2026 industry piece names large AI campuses, such as CloudBurst's 1.2 GW Texas site, that broke ground with no disclosed preleasing. So the claim that all AI data centers have locked-in demand is untrue, as he says. His list of where locked-in demand comes from is a report of his own search and is not scored as complete. SemiAnalysis describes long-term offtakes as dominated by AI labs, often backstopped by hyperscalers, which fits his picture.
limitations: The 'all' framing sets a low bar. Most capacity under construction is preleased, and that share is rising.
CBRE data are not AI-specific and cover only primary North American markets.
The named-customer list is not tested as exhaustive.

our_interpretation: The core claim tested is a rebuttal: it is not true that all AI data centers have locked-in (contracted) customer demand. It holds if a meaningful share of AI data center capacity being built or delivered has no committed tenant or offtaker.

"I can find" makes the named list a report of his own search. It is not scored as a complete list of every committed customer in the market. It is only checked loosely: do public sources describe large long-term commitments as coming mainly from the big cloud companies and the AI labs?
He named no period. The claim describes the state of the market when he wrote. I use the latest reported period before the post: 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-22, which covers first-half 2026 market data.
"Locked-in demand" is read as signed leases, preleases or offtake contracts, not as forecast demand.
criteria.support_condition: Credible market data or reports from the period show that a meaningful share of data center capacity under construction or coming online has no signed tenant, or that developers are building AI campuses on spec without committed customers.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible data show that essentially all AI data center capacity under construction is preleased or contracted. Or public records show widespread long-term commitments from many creditworthy customers outside his list, so that his description of where locked-in demand comes from is plainly misleading.

evidence.excerpt: More than 80% of all capacity under construction is already preleased, up from 74.3% a year ago. This leaves less than 1,500 MW available for pre-leasing across North America's primary markets.
evidence.explanation: Close to a fifth of capacity under construction in the main North American markets (up to about 1,500 MW) had no tenant in H1 2026. So not all capacity being built has locked-in demand. Most of it does, though, and the share is rising.

evidence.excerpt: Applied Digital's Delta Forge 1 campus in Boyce, Louisiana represents the spec build at scale: .6 billion, 300 acres, announced as AI campus infrastructure ahead of named tenants. CloudBurst Data Centers broke ground on a 1.2 GW campus in Central Texas without disclosed pre-leasing.
evidence.locator: section The Projects That Illustrate the Model
evidence.explanation: Names large AI campuses being built before any tenant was named or any preleasing disclosed. These are AI data centers without locked-in customer demand.
